decks.title: Admission of a Partner — Part 1: Ratios and Goodwill
goals: Calculate the new profit-sharing ratio, the sacrificing ratio and any gain by an old partner on admission
Account for goodwill under Accounting Standard 26: premium in cash, retained, withdrawn, in kind, paid privately or not brought (current accounts under fixed capitals)
Write off goodwill already in the books and calculate hidden goodwill

slides.heading: Reconstitution: Admission of a Partner
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **ratios** and **goodwill** when a new partner joins. Every firm, person and figure in this chapter is imagined.

nodes.label: Reconstitution by admission
New, sacrificing and gaining ratios
Premium for goodwill
Goodwill not brought, fixed capitals
Old goodwill and hidden goodwill

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: reconstitution by admission, the new, sacrificing and gaining ratios, premium for goodwill, goodwill not brought with fixed capitals, and old and hidden goodwill
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: When a firm takes in a new partner, the old agreement ends and a new one begins, but the business carries on. This is called reconstitution. The newcomer buys a share in the assets and in the future profits. In this first part we work out the new ratios, see who gives up what, and learn how the old partners are paid for the goodwill they built.

slides.heading: Reconstitution and what must be settled
bullets: Under the **Indian Partnership Act, 1932**, a partner is admitted only with the consent of **all** existing partners (unless the deed says otherwise).
The firm is **reconstituted**, not dissolved: the books are adjusted, not closed.
Six matters are settled before the newcomer shares any profit (see the flow).

nodes.label: New profit-sharing ratio
Sacrificing (and any gaining) ratio
Goodwill
Revaluation Account
Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
Capitals and the new Balance Sheet

visual.alt: Flow of what is settled when a partner is admitted: the new ratio, the sacrificing and any gaining ratio, goodwill, the revaluation account, reserves and accumulated profits or losses, and capitals with the new balance sheet
visual.caption: What is settled on admission

slides.narration: Under the Indian Partnership Act, every existing partner must agree before a newcomer joins. The firm is reconstituted, so we adjust the books instead of closing them. Six matters are settled: the new ratio, the sacrificing ratio and any gain, goodwill, revaluation, reserves and past profits or losses, and finally the capitals and the new balance sheet. This part covers the first three.

slides.heading: Where the new partner's share comes from

headers: New share of an old partner
rows: Share taken in the old ratio
Each surrenders a fraction **of his own share**
Each gives a fraction **of the firm**
Old share − new share (may be negative: a **gain**)

visual.alt: Table of the terms on which a newcomer gets his share: in the old ratio, by surrender of a fraction of one's own share, by giving a fraction of the firm, or with the new ratio stated, when an old partner may even gain; for each it shows the sacrifice and the new share
visual.caption: In every case: sacrifice = old share − new share.

slides.narration: The newcomer's share always comes out of the old shares, but the terms differ. The old partners may give in their old ratio, each may surrender a fraction of his own share, each may give a fraction of the whole firm, or the new ratio may simply be stated. In the last case one old partner may even gain. In every case, sacrifice equals old share minus new share.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: share taken in the old ratio
slides.body_md: Pragati Pickles, Nizamabad (imagined): Sushant and Trupti share **2 : 1**. Udit joins for **1/3**, taken from both in their old ratio.
bullets: Step 1: each old partner keeps 1 − 1/3 = 2/3 of his or her share.
Step 2: multiply, then write every share over one denominator.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 1: Sushant's two thirds becomes four ninths, Trupti's one third becomes two ninths, Udit gets three ninths; the new ratio is 4 : 2 : 3 and the sacrificing ratio 2 : 1
visual.caption: Sacrificing ratio = old ratio 2 : 1.

slides.narration: Udit takes one third, so each old partner keeps two thirds of his or her own share. Sushant's two thirds times two thirds is four ninths. Trupti's one third times two thirds is two ninths. Udit's one third is three ninths. The new ratio is four to two to three, and because both gave in the old ratio, the sacrificing ratio is still two to one.

slides.heading: Quick check: fractions of the firm
slides.body_md: Subtract a fraction of the firm directly.
slides.narration: Each old partner hands over a fraction of the whole profit. Subtract it straight from each old share.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an old partner who gains
slides.body_md: Zoji Woollens, Leh (imagined): Amrita and Bhuvan share **3 : 2**. Cyrus joins, and the new ratio of Amrita, Bhuvan and Cyrus is stated as **1 : 2 : 1**.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 2: Amrita falls from twelve twentieths to five twentieths, a sacrifice of seven twentieths; Bhuvan rises from eight to ten twentieths, a gain of one tenth; Cyrus receives five twentieths
visual.caption: Amrita's 7/20 = Cyrus's 5/20 + Bhuvan's gain 2/20.

slides.narration: Write every share in twentieths. Amrita falls from twelve to five twentieths, a sacrifice of seven twentieths. Bhuvan rises from eight to ten twentieths, so he gains one tenth. Cyrus receives one quarter. Amrita alone gives up enough to cover both Cyrus and Bhuvan, so both of them must pay her for goodwill.

slides.heading: Quick check: can an old partner gain?
slides.body_md: Think about a stated new ratio.
slides.narration: When the new ratio is simply stated, compare each old share with each new share. Can a difference be negative?

slides.heading: Goodwill on admission and Accounting Standard 26
bullets: **Premium for goodwill** = firm's goodwill × newcomer's share.
Only **purchased goodwill** may be recorded, so no goodwill account is raised on admission.

nodes.label: Old partners give up future profits
Newcomer (and any gaining partner) compensates them
Credited to the sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio
No goodwill account raised (Accounting Standard 26)

visual.alt: Flow: old partners give up part of their future profits; the newcomer, and any old partner who gains, compensates them; the amount is credited to the sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio; no goodwill account is raised because Accounting Standard 26 allows only purchased goodwill
visual.caption: Why a premium for goodwill is paid

slides.narration: The old partners built the firm's reputation, and now they give up part of the profits it will earn. So the newcomer, and any old partner who gains, pays them for goodwill. The premium equals the firm's goodwill times the newcomer's share. Accounting Standard twenty-six allows only purchased goodwill to be recorded, so no goodwill account is opened.

slides.heading: Goodwill entries in each situation

rows: Bank A/c Dr. To Premium for Goodwill A/c; Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr. To sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs
No further entry: it stays in the sacrificing partners' capitals
Premium withdrawn by the old partners
Sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Bank A/c
Asset A/c Dr. To Premium for Goodwill A/c and To newcomer's Capital A/c
Newcomer's Current A/c (or Capital A/c) Dr. To sacrificing partners' Current (or Capital) A/cs

visual.alt: Table of goodwill entries on admission: premium in cash goes through the premium for goodwill account to the sacrificing partners; premium retained needs no further entry; premium withdrawn debits their capitals and credits bank; premium in kind debits the asset; premium not brought debits the newcomer's current or capital account; a private payment needs no entry

slides.narration: Premium in cash passes through the premium for goodwill account to the sacrificing partners. If it is retained, nothing more is needed; if withdrawn, their capitals are debited and the bank credited. Premium in kind debits the asset brought. If the newcomer cannot pay, his current account is debited when capitals are fixed. A private payment needs no entry at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: goodwill when an old partner gains
slides.body_md: Zoji Woollens: goodwill is valued at ₹80,000. Cyrus brings his premium in cash; Bhuvan's gain is charged to his capital.

rows: *(Being premium brought in cash by Cyrus)*
*(Being Amrita compensated by Cyrus and by Bhuvan, who gains)*

visual.alt: Journal of worked example 3: bank debited 20,000 rupees for Cyrus's premium; then premium for goodwill 20,000 and Bhuvan's capital 8,000 debited, crediting Amrita's capital 28,000 rupees

slides.narration: Amrita must receive seven twentieths of rupees eighty thousand, that is rupees twenty-eight thousand. Cyrus pays one quarter, rupees twenty thousand, in cash. Bhuvan pays for his gain of one tenth, rupees eight thousand, through his capital account. The two payments together equal Amrita's compensation.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: premium not brought, fixed capitals
slides.body_md: Pragati Pickles keeps **fixed capitals**. Goodwill is valued at ₹90,000; Udit (1/3) cannot bring his premium.

rows: *(Being Udit's share of goodwill adjusted through current accounts in the sacrificing ratio 2 : 1)*

visual.alt: Journal of worked example 4 under fixed capitals: Udit's current account debited 30,000 rupees, crediting Sushant's current account 20,000 and Trupti's 10,000

slides.narration: Udit's share of goodwill is one third of rupees ninety thousand, that is rupees thirty thousand. With fixed capitals, the capital accounts change only for capital introduced or withdrawn, so the adjustment goes through current accounts. Udit's current account is debited, and Sushant and Trupti's current accounts are credited in two to one: rupees twenty thousand and rupees ten thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: fixed capitals and goodwill
slides.body_md: Which accounts carry the adjustment?
slides.narration: With fixed capitals, where do adjustments other than capital introduced go?

slides.heading: Goodwill already in the books
bullets: Old goodwill belongs to the old firm: write it off **first**, in the **old ratio**.
The newcomer's share of the current goodwill is then handled in the usual way.

rows: Written off among the **old partners** in the **old ratio**
Old partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Goodwill A/c
Premium or capital adjustment as usual

visual.alt: Table: goodwill already in the books is first written off by debiting the old partners in the old ratio; the newcomer's share of the current value of goodwill is then dealt with as a premium or capital adjustment in the sacrificing ratio

slides.narration: Sometimes the old balance sheet already shows goodwill. It belongs to the old firm, so it is written off among the old partners in their old ratio before anything else. After that, the newcomer's share of the goodwill valued now is handled as a premium or a capital adjustment in the sacrificing ratio.

slides.heading: Hidden goodwill
slides.body_md: When nothing is said about goodwill, the newcomer's **capital** can reveal it.

nodes.label: Newcomer's capital ÷ his share = implied total capital
minus (old partners' adjusted capitals + newcomer's capital) = hidden goodwill
Hidden goodwill × newcomer's share = his share of goodwill
Debit his capital (or current) account; credit sacrificing partners

visual.alt: Flow for hidden goodwill: divide the newcomer's capital by his share for the implied total capital, subtract the capitals actually in the firm to get hidden goodwill, multiply by his share, and debit him crediting the sacrificing partners
visual.caption: Hidden goodwill in four steps

slides.narration: Sometimes the terms say nothing about goodwill, but the newcomer agrees to bring a capital that is large for his share. Divide his capital by his share to get the capital the firm is worth to him. Subtract the capitals actually in the firm after his admission. The difference is hidden goodwill, and his share of it is charged to him and credited to the sacrificing partners.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: hidden goodwill
slides.body_md: Yercaud Coffee Roasters (imagined): Kartik and Malini share **3 : 1**; capitals after adjustments ₹1,30,000 and ₹70,000. Nimisha joins for **1/5** with ₹75,000, no premium.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 5: implied capital 3,75,000, actual capital 2,75,000, hidden goodwill 1,00,000, Nimisha's share 20,000 credited to Kartik 15,000 and Malini 5,000 rupees
visual.caption: Entry: Nimisha's Capital A/c Dr. ₹20,000 To Kartik's Capital A/c ₹15,000 and Malini's Capital A/c ₹5,000.

slides.narration: Nimisha's rupees seventy-five thousand for one fifth values the capital at rupees three lakh seventy-five thousand. The capitals actually in the firm add up to rupees two lakh seventy-five thousand. So hidden goodwill is rupees one lakh, and Nimisha's fifth, rupees twenty thousand, is debited to her and credited to Kartik and Malini in three to one.

slides.heading: Quick check: hidden goodwill
slides.body_md: Implied capital, minus actual capital, times the new share.
slides.narration: Follow the four steps of the flow and give your answer in rupees.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Old share − new share; a negative result is a gain
Sacrificing partners, in the sacrificing ratio
Pays for his gain, like the newcomer
Debit newcomer's current account (fixed capitals) or capital account
Write off in the old ratio

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: sacrifice is old share minus new share, negative meaning a gain; premium is goodwill times the newcomer's share and goes to sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio; a gaining old partner also pays; premium not brought is debited to the newcomer; old goodwill is written off in the old ratio; hidden goodwill comes from the capitals

slides.narration: To sum up: each sacrifice is old share minus new share, and a negative result is a gain. The premium for goodwill is the firm's goodwill times the newcomer's share and goes to the sacrificing partners. A gaining old partner pays as well. If the premium is not brought, the newcomer is charged. Old goodwill is written off in the old ratio, and hidden goodwill is read from the capitals.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always **show the sacrificing ratio**; it often differs from the old ratio.
Read the wording: a fraction **of his own share** is multiplied; a fraction **of the firm** is subtracted.
If the new ratio is stated, check every partner: an old partner may **gain** and must pay for it.
With **fixed capitals**, goodwill adjustments go through **current accounts**.
Write a **narration** under every entry, and never open a goodwill account for the premium.
slides.narration: A few habits save marks. Show the sacrificing ratio every time. Read whether a partner gives a fraction of his own share or of the whole firm. When the new ratio is stated, check each partner, because one may gain. Remember that fixed capitals push goodwill adjustments into current accounts. And write a narration under every journal entry.

decks.title: Admission of a Partner — Part 2: Revaluation, Reserves, Capitals and Change in Ratio
goals: Prepare the Revaluation Account and share its result among the old partners
Close reserves and accumulated profits or losses, or keep them with a single adjustment entry
Prepare the capital accounts and the new Balance Sheet in horizontal form, adjusting capitals where agreed
Pass the adjustment entries when existing partners change their profit-sharing ratio

slides.heading: Revaluation, reserves, capitals and change in ratio
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **Revaluation Account**, **reserves**, the **capital accounts**, the **Balance Sheet** in horizontal form, adjusting **capitals**, and a **change in ratio** among existing partners.

nodes.label: Revaluation Account
Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
Capital accounts
New Balance Sheet (horizontal)
Adjusting capitals
Change in ratio among existing partners

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: revaluation account, reserves and accumulated profits or losses, capital accounts, the new balance sheet in horizontal form, adjusting capitals, and a change in ratio among existing partners
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In the first part we settled ratios and goodwill. Now we bring the books up to date before the newcomer steps in. We revalue assets and liabilities, deal with reserves and past profits or losses, prepare the capital accounts and the new balance sheet, adjust capitals, and finally see the same ideas at work when partners simply change their ratio.

slides.heading: Why revalue before admission?
bullets: Book values may be **out of date**: buildings rise, machines wear out, bills go unrecorded.
Gains and losses up to admission belong to the **old partners**, in the **old ratio**.

nodes.label: Book values are out of date
Revalue assets, reassess liabilities
Gain or loss belongs to the old firm
Old partners, old ratio

visual.alt: Flow: book values are out of date, so assets are revalued and liabilities reassessed; the gain or loss belongs to the old firm and goes to the old partners in the old ratio
visual.caption: Why revalue first

slides.narration: The books show historical figures, which may be far from real values on the day of admission. A building may have risen in value, a machine may be worth less, and a bill may be unrecorded. If we ignored these, the newcomer would share gains or losses that arose before he joined. So we revalue first and give the result to the old partners.

slides.heading: The Revaluation Account
columns:
**Debit (losses)**

- Fall in an asset
- Rise in a liability
- Unrecorded liability
- New provision

**Credit (gains)**

- Rise in an asset
- Fall in a liability
- Unrecorded asset
- Provision released

rows: Fall in the value of an asset
Rise in the value of an asset
Balance: profit to old partners (old ratio)
Balance: loss to old partners (old ratio)

visual.alt: Table of the revaluation account: debit side for falls in assets, rises in liabilities, unrecorded liabilities and new provisions, with a profit balance to the old partners; credit side for rises in assets, falls in liabilities and unrecorded assets, with a loss balance to the old partners
visual.caption: Also called the Profit and Loss Adjustment Account.

slides.narration: The revaluation account works like a small profit and loss account. Anything that lowers the worth of the old firm goes on the debit side: a fall in an asset, a rise in a liability, an unrecorded liability or a new provision. Anything that raises it goes on the credit side. The balance is a profit or a loss of the old partners in their old ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: the starting balance sheet
slides.body_md: Konark Stone Carvers, Puri (imagined): Prabhat and Rohini share **3 : 2**. Sanjana joins on 1 April 2026 for **1/4**, taken in the old ratio. She brings ₹1,10,000 as capital and her premium in cash (goodwill ₹1,20,000).

visual.alt: Balance sheet of Konark Stone Carvers before admission, totalling 3,20,000 rupees: creditors, general reserve and the capitals of Prabhat and Rohini; bank, debtors, stock, machinery and building
visual.caption: Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026 (horizontal form).

slides.narration: Here is the balance sheet of Konark Stone Carvers just before Sanjana joins, in horizontal form, with liabilities on the left and assets on the right. Note the general reserve of rupees twenty thousand: it belongs to Prabhat and Rohini. Sanjana takes one quarter in the old ratio, so the sacrificing ratio is three to two.

slides.heading: Worked example 6 (continued): Revaluation Account
slides.body_md: Building up by ₹25,000; machinery down 10%; a 5% provision on debtors; an unrecorded electricity bill of ₹1,500.

rows: To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c

visual.alt: Revaluation account of Konark Stone Carvers: debit side machinery 8,000, provision 2,500 and outstanding electricity 1,500; credit side building 25,000; profit 13,000 rupees shared Prabhat 7,800 and Rohini 5,200

slides.narration: Put the losses on the debit side: machinery eight thousand, the provision two thousand five hundred and the electricity bill one thousand five hundred. The gain on the building, twenty-five thousand, goes on the credit side. The credit side is larger by rupees thirteen thousand, a profit. Prabhat takes three fifths, rupees seven thousand eight hundred, and Rohini two fifths, rupees five thousand two hundred.

slides.heading: Quick check: a gain on revaluation
slides.body_md: Which side does it go on?
slides.narration: Ask yourself whether the item raises or lowers the worth of the old firm.

slides.heading: Reserves and accumulated profits or losses

headers: Item in the old balance sheet
rows: General reserve, credit balance of profit and loss
Single entry: newcomer's Capital A/c Dr. (his share of the net) To sacrificing partners
Debit balance of profit and loss, deferred revenue expenditure
Reduces the net figure in the same single entry
Claim first; balance credited (excess claim: revaluation loss)
Fall first; balance credited (excess fall: revaluation loss)

visual.alt: Table of reserves on admission: reserves and credit balances are credited, and accumulated losses and deferred revenue expenditure debited, to the old partners in the old ratio; if they are kept in the books, one entry debits the newcomer with his share of the net and credits the sacrificing partners; special reserves first meet the claim or the fall

slides.narration: Reserves and undistributed profits were earned by the old partners, so they are credited to them in the old ratio, and accumulated losses are debited the same way. If the partners prefer to keep these items in the books, one entry does the job: the newcomer is debited with his share of the net figure, and the sacrificing partners are credited. Special reserves first meet the claim or the fall.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: closed or kept
slides.body_md: Dhauli Agarbatti Works, Bhubaneswar (imagined): Tapan and Usha share **2 : 1**; Vikas joins for **1/4** (old ratio). General reserve ₹36,000; debit balance of profit and loss ₹6,000.

rows: To Tapan's Capital A/c / Usha's Capital A/c
Tapan's Capital A/c / Usha's Capital A/c Dr.
To Tapan's Capital A/c / Usha's Capital A/c

visual.alt: Table of worked example 7: if closed, the general reserve of 36,000 is credited 24,000 and 12,000 and the loss of 6,000 debited 4,000 and 2,000; if kept, Vikas is debited 7,500 rupees, one quarter of the net 30,000, credited 5,000 and 2,500

slides.narration: If the items are closed, the reserve of rupees thirty-six thousand is credited two to one and the loss of rupees six thousand debited two to one. If they are kept, the net is rupees thirty thousand. Vikas's quarter of it, rupees seven thousand five hundred, is debited to him and credited to Tapan and Usha in their sacrificing ratio. Both methods leave the old partners equally well off.

slides.heading: Quick check: who owns the reserve?
slides.body_md: Think about when the reserve was earned.
slides.narration: Was the reserve built before or after the new partner joined?

slides.heading: The partners' capital accounts
slides.body_md: Prepare them in **columnar form**, one column per partner, newcomer included.

nodes.label: Balance b/d (old partners)
+ revaluation profit, reserves, premium
− revaluation loss, accumulated losses, old goodwill written off
+ capital brought by the newcomer
± surplus or shortfall if capitals are adjusted
Balance c/d → new Balance Sheet

visual.alt: Flow of entries in the partners' capital accounts: opening balances; plus revaluation profit, reserves and premium; minus losses and old goodwill; plus the newcomer's capital; plus or minus capital adjustments; closing balances to the new balance sheet
visual.caption: Order of entries in the capital accounts

slides.narration: All the adjustments meet in the partners' capital accounts, kept in columnar form. Start with the opening balances. Credit the old partners with revaluation profit, reserves and premium, and debit them with losses and any old goodwill. Credit the newcomer with his capital. Capital adjustments, if any, come last, and the closing balances go to the new balance sheet.

slides.heading: Worked example 6 (continued): capital accounts
slides.body_md: Credits to the old partners: revaluation profit, general reserve (3 : 2) and premium (sacrificing ratio 3 : 2).

visual.alt: Partners' capital accounts of Konark Stone Carvers: Prabhat and Rohini credited with revaluation profit, general reserve and premium; Sanjana credited 1,10,000; closing balances Prabhat 1,87,800, Rohini 1,25,200 and Sanjana 1,10,000 rupees

slides.narration: Prabhat and Rohini receive three credits each: the revaluation profit, the general reserve in three to two, and the premium of rupees thirty thousand in their sacrificing ratio, also three to two. Sanjana is credited with her capital. The closing balances are rupees one lakh eighty-seven thousand eight hundred for Prabhat, rupees one lakh twenty-five thousand two hundred for Rohini and rupees one lakh ten thousand for Sanjana.

slides.heading: Worked example 6 (continued): the new Balance Sheet
slides.body_md: Horizontal form; revised values; reserve removed; bank increased by everything Sanjana brought.

visual.alt: Balance sheet of Konark Stone Carvers after Sanjana's admission, in horizontal form, totalling 4,74,500 rupees: creditors, the outstanding electricity bill and three capitals on the left; bank 1,70,000, debtors net of provision, stock, machinery and building at revised values on the right
visual.caption: Reserve gone, revised values in, bank up by everything Sanjana brought.

sections.heading: 1. Reconstitution and admission
sections.body_md:
Any change in the agreement among partners **reconstitutes** the firm: the old agreement ends and a new one begins, but the firm continues and its books are adjusted, not closed. Admission of a partner, a change in the profit-sharing ratio among existing partners, and retirement or death are all reconstitutions.

Under the **Indian Partnership Act, 1932**, a new partner can be admitted only with the consent of all existing partners, unless the deed provides otherwise. The newcomer acquires a **share in the assets** and a **share in the future profits** of the firm.

**Matters settled on admission:** new ratio; sacrificing (and any gaining) ratio; goodwill; revaluation; reserves and accumulated profits or losses; capitals and the new Balance Sheet.

*Not in the ISC 2027 syllabus for this chapter:* memorandum revaluation account, joint life and individual life policies, and admission of a partner during an accounting year.

| Fraction **of his own share** surrendered | Sacrifice = old share × fraction |
| Fraction **of the firm** given | Sacrifice = that fraction |
| New ratio stated | Old share − new share for each partner (an old partner may gain) |

**Checks:** new shares add up to 1; sacrifices minus any gains equal the newcomer's share.

sections.heading: 3. Goodwill on admission (Accounting Standard 26)
sections.body_md:
**Premium for goodwill = firm's goodwill × newcomer's share**, credited to the **sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio**. An old partner who gains pays for his gain in the same way. Accounting Standard 26 allows only purchased goodwill to be recorded, so **no goodwill account** is raised on admission.

- **In cash:** Bank A/c Dr. To Premium for Goodwill A/c; Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr. To sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs.
- **Retained:** no further entry.
- **Withdrawn:** sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Bank A/c.
- **In kind:** Asset A/c Dr. To Premium for Goodwill A/c and To newcomer's Capital A/c.
- **Not brought (wholly or partly):** newcomer's Current A/c (fixed capitals) or Capital A/c (fluctuating) Dr. To sacrificing partners' Current or Capital A/cs.
- **Paid privately:** no entry.

sections.heading: 4. Goodwill already in the books, and hidden goodwill
sections.body_md:

sections.heading: 5. The Revaluation Account
sections.body_md:
The **Revaluation Account** (Profit and Loss Adjustment Account) records changes in values on admission.

- **Debit:** fall in assets, rise in liabilities, unrecorded liabilities, new provisions.
- **Credit:** rise in assets, fall in liabilities, unrecorded assets, provisions released.
- **Balance:** profit credited (or loss debited) to the **old partners** in the **old ratio**.

Typical entries: Revaluation A/c Dr. To Machinery A/c (fall); Building A/c Dr. To Revaluation A/c (rise); Revaluation A/c Dr. To old partners' Capital A/cs (profit).

sections.heading: 6. Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
sections.body_md:
**If closed** (the usual case), in the **old ratio**:
- General reserve, credit balance of profit and loss: Reserve A/c Dr. To old partners' Capital A/cs.
- Debit balance of profit and loss, deferred revenue expenditure (e.g. advertisement suspense): old partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To the account.
- Workmen compensation reserve: meets the claim first; the balance is credited; an excess claim is a revaluation loss.
- Investment fluctuation reserve: meets the fall in investments first; the balance is credited; an excess fall is a revaluation loss.

**If kept in the books** (single adjustment entry): net = reserves + credit balances − accumulated losses; Newcomer's Capital A/c Dr. (net × his share) To sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs (sacrificing ratio).

sections.body_md:
**Capital accounts** are prepared in columnar form for all partners; closing balances go to the new Balance Sheet.

**Old capitals on the basis of the newcomer's capital**
- Total capital = newcomer's capital ÷ his share; required capital = total × each old partner's new share.
- Surplus: withdrawn (Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c) or credited to the current account; shortfall: brought in (Bank A/c Dr. To Capital A/c) or debited to the current account.

**Newcomer's capital on the basis of the old capitals**
- Total = old partners' adjusted capitals ÷ their combined new share; newcomer's capital = total × his share.

**New Balance Sheet:** horizontal form, liabilities and capitals on the left, assets on the right; revised values; reserves removed if closed; closing capitals and any current-account balances shown.

sections.heading: 8. Change in profit-sharing ratio among existing partners
sections.body_md:

- **Revaluation:** profit or loss shared in the **old ratio**.
- **Reserves closed:** shared in the **old ratio**.
- **Reserves kept:** Gaining partner Dr. To sacrificing partner, with (old − new) × net reserves.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Crediting the premium in the **old ratio** when the sacrificing ratio is different.
- Ignoring an old partner who **gains** under a stated new ratio.
- Multiplying when a partner gives a fraction **of the firm**, or subtracting when he surrenders a fraction **of his own share**.
- Giving the newcomer a share of revaluation profit or of reserves earned before he joined.
- Posting goodwill adjustments to fixed capital accounts instead of **current accounts**.
- Comparing capitals before **all** adjustments (revaluation, reserves, premium) are made.
- Drawing the Balance Sheet in vertical form; partnership reconstitution uses the **horizontal** form.

**How marks are usually awarded (SOYL chapter tests on the ISC default pattern)**
- 1 mark: objective items.
- 2 marks: a ratio calculation, or two or three entries with narrations.
- 3 marks: a Revaluation Account, a hidden-goodwill working with its entry, or a set of reserve entries.
- 5 marks in parts, e.g. (a) 2 + (b) 3: ratios and goodwill entries, or a Revaluation Account with capital accounts.
- Full practical (practice, 8 marks): Revaluation Account about 2, capital accounts about 3, Balance Sheet about 3; working notes earn step marks.

questions.stem_md: The partners of an imagined pottery firm at Khurda agree to take in a third partner while the business carries on as before. In partnership accounts this event is

options.text_md: a dissolution of the firm, which closes its books and settles every account
a reconstitution of the firm: the old agreement ends and a new one begins, but the firm is not dissolved
a conversion of the firm into a company under the Companies Act, 2013
a change of name only, which needs no adjustment in the books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a reconstitution of the firm: the old agreement ends and a new one begins, but the firm is not dissolved. Any change in the relationship among the partners, such as an admission, reconstitutes the firm. The business continues, so its books are adjusted for the new agreement rather than closed.

questions.stem_md: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the partners of an imagined spice firm can admit a new partner, unless their deed provides otherwise, only with

options.text_md: the consent of the partner with the largest capital
a majority vote of the existing partners
the permission of the Registrar of Firms
the consent of all the existing partners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the consent of all the existing partners. Section 31 of the Act makes the consent of every existing partner necessary, because the newcomer becomes an agent of each of them.

questions.stem_md: In Malabar Spice House, an imagined export firm at Kozhikode, Anirudh and Bhavya divide profits 5 : 3. Chandan joins with a 1/4 share, which he acquires from the two of them in the ratio in which they already share. After his admission the profit-sharing ratio of Anirudh, Bhavya and Chandan is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 15 : 9 : 8. Each old partner keeps 3/4 of his or her own share: Anirudh 5/8 × 3/4 = 15/32 and Bhavya 3/8 × 3/4 = 9/32, while Chandan's 1/4 is 8/32.

questions.stem_md: Damini and Eshwar run Belgaum Courier Point, an imagined franchise at Belagavi, sharing profits 2 : 1. Falguni is taken in for a 1/6 share, and each old partner hands her 1/12 of the firm's profit. The new ratio of Damini, Eshwar and Falguni is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 7 : 3 : 2. A fraction of the firm's profit is subtracted directly: Damini 2/3 − 1/12 = 7/12, Eshwar 1/3 − 1/12 = 1/4 and Falguni 1/6; over twelve these are 7, 3 and 2.

questions.stem_md: Vedika and Yatin own an imagined boat-repair yard at Kakinada in equal shares. On admitting Zubair they fix the profit-sharing ratio of Vedika, Yatin and Zubair at 3 : 1 : 1. The share of profit given up by Yatin is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 3/10. Yatin falls from 1/2 to 1/5, a sacrifice of 3/10. Vedika rises from 1/2 to 3/5 and gains 1/10, so Yatin's sacrifice covers Zubair's 1/5 and Vedika's gain.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the admission agreement of an imagined firm states the new profit-sharing ratio directly, one old partner may end up with a larger share than before while another old partner gives up more than the newcomer receives.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Old share minus new share can be negative for one partner. The sacrificing partner then gives up enough to cover both the newcomer's share and the other old partner's gain, and both of them compensate him for goodwill.

questions.stem_md: Jyoti and Keshav run Kittur Offset, an imagined printing shop at Hubballi, and split profits 4 : 1. To admit Lavanya, Jyoti hands over 1/4 of her own share and Keshav hands over 1/2 of his own share. In the first year of the new firm the profit is ₹2,40,000. What is Keshav's share of this profit (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Keshav keeps 1/5 − 1/10 = 1/10 of the profit (he gives up half of 1/5), so his share = 2,40,000 × 1/10 = 24,000, that is ₹24,000.

questions.stem_md: When the partners of an existing firm only change their profit-sharing ratio, the ratio in which the partners whose shares rise acquire their extra shares is called the ___ ratio.
questions.solution_md: It is the gaining ratio: new share minus old share for each partner whose share rises.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the admission agreement of an imagined firm states the new profit-sharing ratio directly, the sacrificing ratio has to be worked out and may differ from the old ratio.

**Reason (R):** Each old partner's sacrifice is his old share minus his new share, and these differences need not stand in the proportion of the old shares.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R is why A holds: the sacrifices follow from comparing the two ratios, not from the old ratio alone.

questions.stem_md: Mrinal and Nayana share the profits of Karnal Highway Dhabas, an imagined restaurant chain, 2 : 1. They admit Omprakash for 1/4 share: Mrinal gives him 1/12 of the firm's profit and Nayana gives him 1/6 of the firm's profit. Calculate the new profit-sharing ratio and the sacrificing ratio.
questions.solution_md: Fractions of the firm are subtracted directly from each old share; the sacrificing ratio is the ratio of the fractions given.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. New shares: Mrinal 2/3 − 1/12 = 7/12; Nayana 1/3 − 1/6 = 1/6; Omprakash 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4.
2. New ratio (Mrinal : Nayana : Omprakash) = **7 : 2 : 3**; sacrificing ratio (Mrinal : Nayana) = **1 : 2**.

questions.stem_md: Pallav, Rukmini and Shivam share the profits of Saptagiri Silks, an imagined saree showroom at Tirupati, 3 : 2 : 1. Tejas is admitted for 1/4 share: Pallav and Rukmini each give him 1/8 of the firm's profit and Shivam keeps his share unchanged. Calculate the new profit-sharing ratio and the sacrificing ratio.
questions.solution_md: Bring every share to the common denominator 24 before writing the ratio; a partner who gives nothing drops out of the sacrificing ratio.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. New shares: Pallav 1/2 − 1/8 = 3/8; Rukmini 1/3 − 1/8 = 5/24; Shivam 1/6 − 0 = 1/6; Tejas 1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4.
2. New ratio (Pallav : Rukmini : Shivam : Tejas) = **9 : 5 : 4 : 6**; sacrificing ratio (Pallav : Rukmini) = **1 : 1**.
3. Shivam gives up nothing, so he has no part in the sacrificing ratio. Check: 9 + 5 + 4 + 6 = 24 parts.

questions.stem_md: Girish and Hamsa are equal partners in Kakinada Marine Works, an imagined ship-chandling firm. **Working notes**

2. New ratio (Girish : Hamsa : Indrajit) = **3 : 1 : 1**; only Hamsa sacrifices (3/10); Girish gains 1/10.
3. Hamsa must receive 60,000 × 3/10 = ₹18,000: Indrajit pays 60,000 × 1/5 = ₹12,000 and Girish, a gaining partner, pays 60,000 × 1/10 = ₹6,000.

questions.stem_md: The goodwill of Rann Salt Works, an imagined firm at Gandhidham, is to be valued at two years' purchase of its average profit of ₹45,000. Urvashi is admitted for a 1/5 share and will bring her share of goodwill in cash. The premium she brings is

questions.stem_md: On admission to Nilachal Handlooms, an imagined weaving firm at Sambalpur, the new partner brings a premium for goodwill in cash and the old partners leave it in the business. The premium finally appears in

options.text_md: a goodwill account shown among the assets of the new firm
the new partner's capital account, as part of his capital
the profit and loss appropriation account of the year
the old partners' capital accounts, credited in their sacrificing ratio

questions.stem_md: Vinay, joining an imagined interior-design studio at Puducherry, pays his share of goodwill directly to the two old partners from his personal savings, outside the studio. In the books of the studio this payment is

options.text_md: credited to the old partners' capital accounts in their sacrificing ratio
not recorded at all; only the capital he brings into the studio is entered
debited to Vinay's capital account and credited to a goodwill account
recorded through a premium for goodwill account and then closed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** not recorded at all; only the capital he brings into the studio is entered. The money never enters the studio's cash or bank, so the firm has nothing to record for it.

questions.stem_md: The partners of Tawi Dry Fruits, an imagined firm at Jammu, keep fixed capitals. A new partner cannot bring his share of goodwill in cash. To adjust it, the firm

options.text_md: debits the new partner's current account and credits the sacrificing partners' current accounts
debits the new partner's fixed capital account and credits a goodwill account
debits a goodwill account and credits all partners' capital accounts in the new ratio
debits the sacrificing partners' current accounts and credits the new partner's current account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** debits the new partner's current account and credits the sacrificing partners' current accounts. questions.stem_md: Instead of cash, a new partner in Chilika Prawn Farms, an imagined aquaculture firm in Odisha, brings an aerator system whose agreed value covers both his capital and his premium for goodwill. The aerator system is

debited to a goodwill account and credited to the old partners
recorded at the amount of his capital only, leaving the premium out of the books

questions.stem_md: A partner of an imagined travel agency at Darjeeling suggests raising goodwill in the books at its full value when a new partner joins. State how goodwill is treated on admission under Accounting Standard 26 (Intangible Assets), and give one reason why his suggestion cannot be followed.
questions.solution_md: Answer in two steps: what is done instead of raising goodwill, then the standard's rule on self-generated goodwill.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Treatment:** no goodwill account is raised. The new partner's share of goodwill is brought as a premium and credited to the sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio; if he cannot bring it, his capital (or current) account is debited and the sacrificing partners are credited.

**Reason:** the standard allows only **purchased goodwill** to be recognised. Goodwill the firm has built up itself has no cost that can be measured reliably, so it cannot be shown as an asset.

the new partner's capital account with ₹48,000

questions.stem_md: Raunak and Smita share 2 : 1 in Pench Timber Mart, an imagined firm at Seoni, whose books carry goodwill of ₹36,000. Tushar is admitted for 1/4 share, taken from them in their old ratio. The firm's goodwill is now valued at ₹96,000 and Tushar brings his share of it in cash. Pass the journal entries for goodwill.
questions.solution_md: Clear the old goodwill from the books in the old ratio before dealing with the newcomer's premium.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Working notes**

1. Nalini takes 1/5 from the old partners in their old ratio, so each old partner keeps 4/5 of his or her share: Lalitha 3/4 × 4/5 = 3/5; Mukund 1/4 × 4/5 = 1/5; Nalini 1/5.
